opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, because I've worked on both sides of the border.

In some ways the two systems look very different, but when it comes to data they share more problems than you'd expect. In the US, the system is fragmented by design. You have private insurers, large hospital networks, small practices, and each of them runs its own electronic health record, often from a different vendor. The data exists, and there's a lot of it, but it sits in silos. Interoperability has improved, partly because of federal pressure and incentive programs, but moving a patient's full record between institutions is still harder than it should be. On the other hand, the size of some of those networks means that a single health system can hold millions of records. That's a big advantage for research and for building machine learning models.

People often assume Canada should have an easier time, since we have a single-payer system. The reality is that health care is a provincial responsibility, so we really have thirteen separate systems, each with its own data infrastructure, privacy legislation, and governance processes. Inside a province, especially in places like Ontario or Alberta, you can sometimes get remarkably complete, population-level data, because nearly everyone is in the same system. That's a real strength. But doing research across provinces, or linking data between them, can mean months or even years of approvals and agreements.

So the common thread is that the technical barriers are usually not the hardest part anymore. The hard part is governance: who owns the data, who is allowed to access it, under what conditions, and how you keep patients' trust while doing it. I think both countries are still working out how to share data responsibly so it can actually improve care, and not just sit locked away. That's also where I see a lot of opportunity for approaches like federated learning and other privacy-preserving methods, where models can learn from data across institutions without the raw data ever leaving its home.

r001.rationale: It contrasts Canada’s thirteen province-based systems with a fragmented U.S. landscape where hospitals, practices, and networks often use separate records and data silos.

r002.rationale: It identifies governance, approvals, and interoperability as barriers, but does not say U.S. hospitals lack knowledge about how to share patient data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that in both countries, the systems were never really designed around the patient. They were designed around billing, around institutions, around whoever happened to buy the record system at a given hospital. So what you end up with is data that's fragmented along boundaries that have nothing to do with how a person actually moves through care.

In the United States, that fragmentation shows up as a market problem. You have many competing vendors, many competing health systems, and the incentives to share are weak because the data is treated as an asset. In Canada, it's more of a jurisdictional problem. Health care is provincial, so you have thirteen different approaches, and even within a province you'll have one record system in the cancer center and a different one in the community hospital down the road. A patient with cancer who gets imaging in one place, surgery in another, and chemotherapy somewhere else has their story scattered across all of those.

For someone doing the kind of work I do, building models from imaging and clinical records, that matters enormously. The hardest part of a project is almost never the algorithm. It's assembling a coherent, longitudinal picture of a patient from pieces that were never meant to fit together. We spend an enormous amount of effort just reconciling identifiers, harmonizing formats, and figuring out which record is the ground truth.

Where I'd push back on the usual framing is that I don't think the answer is one giant national database. I think it's agreeing on standards and on the terms under which data can move, so that the systems can talk to each other and patients can actually see and direct what's happening with their information. The technology to do that exists. What's lagging is the governance and the trust. And I'd say Canada actually has an advantage there, because a single-payer system gives you a natural place to make those decisions, if there's the will to use it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Canada’s provincial organization with US fragmentation tied to competing systems and records chosen by individual hospitals.

r002.rationale: It attributes US sharing difficulties to weak incentives and data being treated as an asset, but does not identify hospitals’ lack of knowledge about how to share data.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the biggest challenges in both Canada and the United States is that patient data is fragmented. A patient experiences their health as one continuous story, but their information can be spread across hospitals, family practices, and different electronic systems that don’t necessarily communicate well.

Canada’s publicly funded system doesn’t automatically mean we have a unified patient record. And in the United States, information can be divided across providers and insurance networks. In either case, bringing that information together so it can support care and research is difficult.

The goal shouldn’t simply be to share everything. It should be to make the right information available for a clear purpose, with privacy protections and governance that patients can trust.

r001.rationale: The response says data is fragmented in both countries, but does not contrast Canada’s province-based organization with the United States’ hospital-by-hospital organization.

r002.rationale: The response describes systems that do not communicate well, but does not identify US hospitals’ lack of knowledge about how to share data as a barrier.

sol-6.1.text: I think one of the biggest challenges in both Canada and the United States is that patient data is fragmented. You might imagine that your health information follows you wherever you receive care, but it often sits in separate systems that don’t communicate well with one another. Canada has publicly funded health care, but that doesn’t mean we have one unified patient record. And in the United States, you have different institutions and networks with their own systems. That makes it difficult to bring together a complete picture of a patient’s health. The opportunity is to make that information useful across those boundaries while protecting patients’ privacy.
